query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten-based laminated composites for fusion plasma-facing components, embedding a coherent, micron-scale transition metal layer (specifically vanadium) at the tungsten interface enhances high‐temperature plastic strain and toughness by facilitating dislocation transmission across an optimized W–TiN interface and reducing stress concentrations that lead to brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W/TiN/Ta composite without a designed transition metal layer, exhibiting limited ductility and toughness at high operating temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled micron-scale vanadium (V) layer to form a W/V/TiN/Ta laminated composite using uniform processing conditions (e.g., spark plasma sintering) to ensure comparable microstructures apart from the added V layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing conditions that simulate fusion reactor environments (e.g., room temperature up to 800°C or above) under both flexural and tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent V layer at the tungsten interface acts as a mediator by forming an optimized interfacial bond that improves dislocation slip transmission.
generation.mechanism: The V layer reduces interfacial energy and creates a smoother transition between phases, which lowers the barrier for dislocation movement and mitigates stress concentration at the W–TiN interface. This delay in crack initiation under high strain rates improves both plastic strain and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline W/TiN/Ta composite, the W/V/TiN/Ta composite will show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature plastic strain (e.g., on the order of a 17% increase in flexural strain as suggested by prior studies) and improved overall toughness, as evidenced by higher bending strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (plastic strain, flexural strength, toughness) of the unmodified W/TiN/Ta composite serve as the control condition.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis should hold for tungsten-based laminated composites processed via spark plasma sintering and tested under high-temperature mechanical loading conditions relevant to fusion reactor applications. It may not extend to other alloy systems, architectures, or plastic deformation mechanisms (e.g., those dominated by coherent nanoprecipitation in high-entropy alloys).
generation.uncertainty: While the evidence from laminated composites suggests a beneficial effect of a V layer on mechanical properties, the relative contributions of process variables (such as sintering temperature and layer thickness) and potential microstructural heterogeneities remain to be fully disentangled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples under identical processing conditions: one set of conventional W/TiN/Ta composites (control) and one set of W/V/TiN/Ta composites with a micron-scale V layer. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical (flexural and tensile) tests in identical atmospheres mimicking fusion reactor service conditions. Analyze both the macroscopic mechanical properties and the interfacial microstructure using TEM/EPMA.
measurements: Tensile ductility and yield strength at elevated temperatures
Interface microstructure characterization (to confirm the coherence and quality of the V layer)
Dislocation density and distribution via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W/V/TiN/Ta composite does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 17% increase in measured plastic strain and corresponding improvement in toughness parameters) over the control under identical test conditions, or if interface analysis fails to show enhanced dislocation transmission across a coherent transition layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe widespread applications of W in the fusion reactor are limited by its low-temperature brittleness, recrystallization brittleness, and irradiation-induced brittleness. Many toughening methods were used to improve the brittleness of W, such as adding second-phase particles, adding W fibers, preparing laminated composite, and so on. Among these, preparing laminated W-based composites has been proven to effectively improve both the low-temperature and high-temperature toughness of W. In this study, W/M/TiN/Ta-laminated composites with transition metal layer (M) were synthesized through the spark plasma sintering (SPS) at three different temperatures. The effects of nano-scale (Ni, Ti, and Cr) and micron-scale (Ni, Ti, and V) transition layers on the bending and interfacial properties of the W/M/TiN/Ta composite were studied via an electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA) and transmission electron microscope (TEM). Compared with W/TiN/Ta, the flexural strength and strain of W/Ninm/TiN/Ta were increased by 25.6% and 17.6%, respectively.
